summary: ECH keys must be configured into TLS servers, which may use different TLS libraries. This document specifies a PEM file format for them, like RFC 7468.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a standard envelope format for the secret key files, so any server software can read them.

questions: what is an ech pem file
subtitle: A standard PEM file that holds an ECH private key and its public config, so any TLS server can load it.

tldr.problem: Encrypted ClientHello (ECH) key pairs must be configured into TLS servers built with different TLS libraries, and there is no common file format for them.
tldr.mechanism: A PEM ECH file holds zero or one PKCS #8 private key followed by one ECHConfigList in base64, with the PEM label ECHCONFIG for the public part.
tldr.outcome: Different TLS servers can share the same key and config files, in the same spirit as the PEM formats in RFC 7468. The private key must never be published in the DNS.

today: RFC 9934 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2026. It has not been updated or obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a Common File Format
sections.content:
Encrypted ClientHello (ECH) for TLS 1.3 is a confidentiality mechanism for server names and other ClientHello content. It needs an ECHConfigList published in an HTTPS or SVCB record in the DNS. Each ECHConfig in that list holds the public component of a key pair that a key manager will typically regenerate periodically.

TLS servers then need to be configured with those key pairs. Because servers are built with different TLS libraries, the RFC argues there is a benefit in a standard format, just as RFC 7468 did for other PEM files.
sections.plainLanguage: Different server programs all need the same secret and public keys. A shared file format means they can all read the same file.

sections.title: The ECHConfig PEM File
sections.content:
A PEM ECH file contains zero or one private key and one encoded ECHConfigList. Both parts MUST be PEM encoded. The file is the PEM private key (if present) followed by the PEM public key(s), and the private key MUST be encoded as a PKCS #8 PrivateKey.

The public part MUST be the base64 form of an ECHConfigList value that can be published in the DNS in an HTTPS record, and the string ECHCONFIG MUST be used in its PEM delimiter. Any content after the PEM encoded ECHConfigList SHOULD be ignored.

When a private key is present, the ECHConfigList MUST contain an ECHConfig that matches it. A list may hold several ECHConfig values, for example with different extensions or public_name values, in decreasing order of preference. A server may also use several files, for instance to take retry_configs from only some of them.
sections.plainLanguage: The file has the secret key first and the public key second, each wrapped in labelled lines. The secret key must match one of the public ones.

sections.title: Protecting the Key File
sections.content:
Keys stored in files are vulnerable if anyone gets read access to the filesystem. The RFC says to use the same protection mechanisms that would protect a server's PEM-encoded HTTPS certificate private key.

Only the ECHConfigList is to be published in the DNS. The private key from an ECH PEM file MUST NOT be published in the DNS. The RFC has no IANA actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Treat the secret key like the key to your house: keep the file locked away, and never post it where everyone can see.

data.title: ECHConfig PEM file
data.code:
-----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----
MC4CAQAwBQYDK2VuBCIEICjd4yGRdsoP9gU7YT7My8DHx1Tjme8GYDXrOMCi8v1V
-----END PRIVATE KEY-----
-----BEGIN ECHCONFIG-----
AD7+DQA65wAgACA8wVN2BtscOl3vQheUzHeIkVmKIiydUhDCliA4iyQRCwAEAAEA
AQALZXhhbXBsZS5jb20AAA==
-----END ECHCONFIG-----
